overview.historicalContext:
**From Ambiguity to AI Breakthrough**

Erdos Problem #728 was posed by Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus in 1975. The original formulation was ambiguous - as written, it had trivial solutions. The AlphaProof team noted solutions with very large values of a and b, and the mathematical community debated the intended constraints.

In January 2026, after the problem statement was clarified to require a,b ≤ (1-ε)n, Kevin Barreto prompted GPT-5.2 which produced a complete solution. The proof was then formalized in Lean using Aristotle and simplified by Boris Alexeev.

**Why This Matters**: Unlike Erdos #124 (which used known techniques in a novel combination), this solution appears genuinely new. Terence Tao noted it was 'not replicated in existing literature' - the clearest evidence yet that AI can generate original mathematics.

**See Also**: [Erdos Problem #124](https://www.erdosproblems.com/124) was the first AI-autonomous solution (November 2025). Problem #728 represents the next milestone: AI producing novel mathematical content.
overview.problemStatement:
**Erdos Problem #728 (Clarified)**

Let ε > 0 be small and C, C' > 0. Do there exist infinitely many integer triples (a, b, n) such that:

1. **Range constraints**: a ≥ εn and b ≥ εn
2. **Divisibility**: a! b! | n! (a+b-n)!
3. **Gap condition**: C log n < a+b-n < C' log n

**Background**: Erdos proved that if a!b! | n! then a+b ≤ n + O(log n). This problem asks whether we can find infinitely many examples achieving this logarithmic gap.

**Answer**: YES - for any 0 < C₁ < C₂, there are infinitely many (a,b,n) with b = n/2, a = n/2 + O(log n), and C₁ log n < a+b-n < C₂ log n.

overview.proofStrategy:
**Probabilistic Method with p-adic Analysis**

1. **Kummer's Theorem**: The p-adic valuation of (n choose k) equals the number of carries when adding k and n-k in base p.

2. **Key Insight**: For the divisibility a!b! | n!(a+b-n)!, we need to control p-adic valuations. The term (a+b-n)! in the denominator eliminates obstacles from small primes.

3. **Concentration Bounds**: Use Chernoff-style estimates to show that 'good' values of m (where the divisibility holds) are plentiful in intervals [M, 2M].

4. **Construction**: Set b = m, n = 2m, a = m + k where k ≈ c log m. Show the divisibility condition is satisfied for most m.

5. **Infinitude**: Since good triples exist in every sufficiently large interval, there are infinitely many solutions.
keyInsights: Kummer's theorem translates factorial divisibility into base-p digit carry counting
The (a+b-n)! term in the denominator is crucial - it cancels problematic small prime contributions
The probabilistic method shows most values work, rather than constructing specific examples
Setting b = n/2 and a close to n/2 optimizes the construction
GPT-5.2 independently identified that 'throwing away k!' was problematic and reformulated the argument

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Definitions of W_p (p-adic valuation of the product of m+1..m+k) and kappa_p (p-adic valuation of the central binomial coefficient).

sections.title: Forced Carries Lemma
sections.summary: Key lemma: if p^j divides m+i for sufficiently small i, then kappa_p(m) >= j.

sections.title: Large Prime Analysis
sections.summary: For primes p > 2k, kappa_p(m) >= W_p(m), reducing the analysis to small primes.

sections.title: Counting and Interval Bounds
sections.summary: Definitions of N_pj, J_p, V_p; bounds on the number of multiples of p^j in (m, m+k]; W_p as a sum of N_pj; residue-class counts in [M, 2M]; and the spike count bound for V_p.

sections.title: Digit Lower Bound for kappa
sections.summary: kappa_p(m) is at least the number of base-p digits d_u (u < L) with d_u >= (p+1)/2, connecting carries to the digit expansion.

sections.title: Probabilistic Carry Model
sections.summary: Definitions of eta, theta, mu, L_p, Q_p; concentration of m mod Q with error O(M^{-eta}); and the bound Q_p <= M^{1-eta}.

sections.title: MGF and Chernoff Bound
sections.summary: Moment generating function for the carry count, Markov's inequality, the Chernoff bound P(X_p <= mu/2) <= exp(-mu/8), and the coefficient comparison for log M.

sections.title: Parameter Choices and Bad-Carry Counting
sections.summary: Definitions of k_val and t_val, a lower bound for mu/2 in terms of log M, and the per-prime bound on m with few carries.

sections.title: Erdős Set and Bad-Set Definitions
sections.summary: The set of admissible triples for Erdős #728, the bad-m set (carry or spike failures), and the summed upper bounds for bad counts over primes.

sections.title: Carry-Sum Bounds and Asymptotic Ratios
sections.summary: Splitting the bad-carry bound into term1 and term2, the bound theta >= 1/3, lower bounds for coeff_lhs, and the limiting ratios log M / log(k_val c M) -> infinity.

sections.title: Vanishing of Bad Carries
sections.summary: term2 and the exponential sums tend to 0; sum_bound_carries identity; for large M the number of bad carries is below (M+1)/3; spike bound introduced.

sections.title: Vanishing of Bad Spikes
sections.summary: Spike-term definitions, bounds on sum_spike_term1, the limit sum_p p/p^t -> 0, the bound on sum_spike_term2, and bad spikes below (M+1)/3 for large M.

sections.title: Reduction and Main Inequality
sections.summary: Bounds on k_val (between C log(4M) and (1-2eps)M), the valuation condition for the improved reduction, sufficient divisibility conditions, and the asymptotic main inequality.

sections.title: Good Triple Construction
sections.summary: Unbounded third component implies an infinite set; the weak threshold holds for relevant primes; non-bad m yield valuation conditions; construction of an admissible triple and existence of a good m for any c > 0.

sections.title: Main Theorem
sections.summary: The set of good triples is infinite; erdos_728 and the refined erdos_728_fc establish infinitely many (a,b,n) with a!b! | n!(a+b-n)! in the logarithmic regime.

conclusion.summary: Erdos Problem #728 asked whether infinitely many triples (a,b,n) exist with a!b! | n!(a+b-n)! and a+b exceeding n by a logarithmic amount. The proof uses p-adic analysis and the probabilistic method to show that such triples are abundant. This represents the first genuinely novel mathematical result generated primarily by AI systems.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance:**

**1. Novel AI Mathematics**: Unlike previous AI proofs that combined known techniques, this appears to be genuinely new mathematics.

**2. Probabilistic Number Theory**: Demonstrates the power of concentration inequalities in factorial divisibility problems.

**3. Human-AI Collaboration**: The workflow (GPT-5.2 for insight, Aristotle for formalization, humans for verification) may become standard.

**4. Problem Clarification**: The formal verification process helped disambiguate the original problem statement.

**Related Work**: See [Erdos Problem #124](../erdos-124-complete-sequences) for the first autonomous AI solution, and [erdosproblems.com](https://www.erdosproblems.com/) for the full collection.

mainTheorems.name: erdos_728
mainTheorems.significance: The positive resolution of Erdős problem #728: for every C>0 and every 0<ε<1/2 there are infinitely many triples (a,b,n) with a!·b! ∣ n!·(a+b−n)! obeying the range constraints and a+b > n + C·log n — factorial divisibility persists beyond the logarithmic barrier.
mainTheorems.description: Reduces to producing triples with arbitrarily large n (infinite_of_unbounded_n), then for each N constructs a good triple via the probabilistic-method machinery (lemma_good_triple_construction_final).

mainTheorems.name: erdos_728_fc
mainTheorems.statement: ∀ᶠ ε in 𝓝[>]0, ∀ C>0, ∀ C'>C, ∃ a b n, 0 < n ∧ … (explicit good triple with a+b > n + C'·log n)
mainTheorems.significance: A finitary, fully-quantified companion to erdos_728: for all sufficiently small ε and any threshold C', an explicit good triple exists. This is the constructive existence statement underlying the infinitude result.
mainTheorems.description: Unpacks the eventual-in-ε construction, threading the threshold reduction (lemma_threshold_reduction) and the explicit small-prime/large-prime carry analysis.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_forced_carries_largep
mainTheorems.statement: p prime, 1 ≤ i < p, i ≤ (p−1)/2, p^j ∣ m+i ⟹ κ_p(m) ≥ j
mainTheorems.significance: The large-prime carry engine: if a prime power p^j divides some m+i in a short window, Kummer's theorem forces at least j carries when adding m to m in base p, so v_p(binom(2m,m)) ≥ j. Divisibility of a shifted value is converted into guaranteed p-adic valuation.
mainTheorems.description: Applies Kummer's theorem (padicValNat_choose) to write κ_p(m) as a carry sum, then shows p^j ∣ m+i forces ⌊2m/p^k⌋ − 2⌊m/p^k⌋ ≥ 1 for each k ≤ j via the congruence m ≡ −i (mod p^k).

mainTheorems.name: lemma_p_gt_2k
mainTheorems.significance: For primes larger than the window (2k < p) the binomial valuation dominates the window-valuation W_p(m,k) = v_p((m+1)···(m+k)). Isolates the contribution of large primes to the divisibility.
mainTheorems.description: Case split on whether some m+i (1 ≤ i ≤ k) is divisible by p; if so, lemma_forced_carries_largep supplies the needed carries, otherwise W_p(m,k)=0.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_forced_carries_smallp
mainTheorems.significance: The small-prime counterpart: the binomial valuation dominates the random variable X_p counting favorable residues up to level L. Together with lemma_p_gt_2k this covers all primes and is the deterministic backbone of the probabilistic bound.
mainTheorems.description: Induction reducing κ_p and X_p to their carry/indicator definitions, bounding the valuation below by the count of forced carries at each level.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_chernoff_binomial
mainTheorems.statement: p prime ⟹ (fraction of m ∈ [0,p^L) with X_p(p,m,L) ≤ μ/2) ≤ exp(−μ/8)
mainTheorems.significance: The Chernoff tail bound at the heart of the probabilistic method: the density of 'bad' m for which the carry count falls below half its mean μ decays exponentially. This is what makes the union of bad sets summable.
mainTheorems.description: Combines a Markov exponential-moment bound (lemma_markov_exp) with the numeric inequality lemma_chernoff_inequality to convert the moment bound into the exp(−μ/8) tail.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_chernoff_inequality
mainTheorems.significance: The scalar convexity estimate that powers the Chernoff bound — a clean explicit inequality controlling the exponential moment generating function of the Bernoulli carry indicators.
mainTheorems.description: Proved by nlinarith after unfolding the exponentials, using log 2 < 0.6931… and the elementary bound log x ≤ x − 1.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_mod_uniform
mainTheorems.statement: Q ≤ M^{1−η}, all a ∈ A below Q ⟹ Prob_{[M,2M]}(m mod Q ∈ A) ≤ |A|/Q + 2/M^η
mainTheorems.significance: Equidistribution of residues: on the dyadic block [M,2M] the reduction m mod Q is nearly uniform provided Q is not too large, so the probability of landing in a residue set A is essentially |A|/Q. Supplies the 'randomness' that the probabilistic method exploits.
mainTheorems.description: Counts integers in [M,2M] with m mod Q ∈ A by writing the interval as full periods plus a remainder, bounding the error by 2|A|.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_bad_carries_bound
mainTheorems.significance: Transports the exponential Chernoff density on a full residue period to the working dyadic interval [M,2M], the count that must be summed over all primes and shown negligible.
mainTheorems.description: Feeds the per-period Chernoff bound (lemma_chernoff_binomial) through the near-uniformity estimate (lemma_mod_uniform) to bound the interval count.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_mu_ge
mainTheorems.statement: p prime ⟹ μ_p/2 ≥ (1−η)/2·θ_p·(log M / log p) − θ_p/2
mainTheorems.significance: Lower-bounds the mean carry count μ_p, showing it grows like log M / log p. A large mean is exactly what makes the Chernoff tail exp(−μ/8) small, closing the probabilistic argument.
mainTheorems.description: Rearranges lemma_mu_lower_bound: the expected number of favorable residues over L levels is at least a constant times log M / log p.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_main_ineq_asymptotic
mainTheorems.significance: The decisive asymptotic: the gain (1−η)/6·log M eventually dominates all logarithmic error terms in the window size k, guaranteeing the constructed triples clear the a+b > n + C·log n threshold for large M.
mainTheorems.description: A Tendsto-atTop statement; the linear-in-log-M main term outpaces the O(log k · log log M) corrections as M → ∞.

mainTheorems.name: lemma_good_m_exists_any_c
mainTheorems.statement: c>0 ⟹ ∃ M₀, ∀ M ≥ M₀, ([M,2M] \ bad_m_set M c) is nonempty
mainTheorems.significance: The pigeonhole payoff of the probabilistic method: once the total measure of bad m is < 1, a good m survives in every large dyadic block, yielding the required triple. Converts summable tail bounds into existence.
mainTheorems.description: Uses lemma_sum_bad_carries_small (the summed bad-carry mass tends to 0) so the bad set cannot cover the whole interval [M,2M].

mainTheorems.name: lemma_good_triple_construction_final
mainTheorems.statement: From a good m (all small primes favorable) construct an explicit good triple (a,b,n) satisfying a!b! ∣ n!(a+b−n)! and the range/threshold constraints
mainTheorems.significance: The constructive core: turns a single well-behaved m into an actual factorial-divisibility triple meeting every constraint of problem #728, the object whose infinitude is the theorem.
mainTheorems.description: Assembles the divisibility from the per-prime valuation guarantees (small primes via lemma_small_primes_good, large primes via lemma_p_gt_2k) and Kummer's theorem, then checks the a+b > n + C log n threshold.

mainTheorems.name: infinite_of_unbounded_n
mainTheorems.statement: (∀ N, ∃ t ∈ S, t.2.2 ≥ N) ⟹ S.Infinite
mainTheorems.significance: The clean reduction principle closing the proof: a set of triples containing elements with arbitrarily large third coordinate n must be infinite. Lets the construction focus on producing large-n triples rather than counting them.
mainTheorems.description: Contrapositive: a finite set of naturals is bounded, so if the n-coordinates are unbounded the set cannot be finite.
